nature-res-108.title: Land use change: when forest becomes farm or city
nature-res-108.text: Since farming began, global forest cover has shrunk by 35%. Most of that loss is land use change: a piece of land switching from one land-use category to another, such as forest to cropland. Deforestation has historically been its main driver. Together with burning fossil fuels, it is a major human source of carbon dioxide. Human activity is the biggest cause of changes to what covers the land, and people also feel the consequences. Cities show how far the effects reach. Urban areas cover just 3% of Earth's surface, but their rising consumption drives land change far away. The starkest example is the Aral Sea. A Soviet irrigation diversion cost it 85% of its area and 90% of its volume, and its fishery collapsed. Every switch in land use, in other words, changes what the land can give back.

nature-res-093.title: Sustainable forest management: three pillars in balance
nature-res-093.text: Forest under management plans grew by 365 million hectares after 1990, reaching 2.13 billion hectares, 55% of all forest, in 2025. Sustainable forest management means running forests on the principles of {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. It must balance three pillars: ecological, economic and sociocultural. The payoffs range from protecting local livelihoods and biodiversity to reducing rural poverty and easing some effects of climate change. Goals differ by forest. Biodiversity conservation is the main aim in around 13% of the world's forests, and protecting soil and water in more than 30%. The {{ref:nature-gov-136}}, adopted at the 1992 Rio summit known as the {{ref:nature-hist-003}}, captured how the world understood it at that time.

nature-res-090.title: Economic water scarcity: plenty of water, no pipes
nature-res-090.text: A quarter of the world's population lives with economic water scarcity, much of Sub-Saharan Africa among them. Their problem is not a lack of water. It is too little investment in the infrastructure or technology needed to draw water from rivers, aquifers and other sources. It also reflects weak human capacity to meet demand. The UN Development Programme calls it the most common cause of water scarcity, because most regions have enough water but lack the means to deliver it. The cost falls on daily life. People without reliable access may walk long distances to fetch water, which is often unclean.

nature-res-089.title: Physical water scarcity: when nature runs dry
nature-res-089.text: Around a fifth of the world's population lives in regions where there simply is not enough water. Physical water scarcity occurs when natural water resources cannot meet all demands, including the water ecosystems need. Dry regions, such as those with a desert climate, often suffer from it. Central Asia, West Asia, North Africa and most of Australia are examples of such arid areas. The split between physical and {{ref:nature-res-090}} was first defined in a 2007 study, led by the International Water Management Institute, of 50 years of farm water use.

nature-res-142.title: Land grabbing: the global rush for farmland
nature-res-142.text: The 2007–08 world food price crisis set off a scramble for land. It sparked a sharp rise in mostly foreign agricultural investment in the Global South, to grow industrial food and biofuels. Land grabbing is the large-scale buying or leasing of land by domestic or foreign companies, governments and individuals. Investors fall into three broad types: agribusinesses, governments and speculators. Food-driven deals make up roughly 37% of land investments worldwide, and biofuel production about 21%. Securing water is usually central to these deals, which has produced a related trend called water grabbing. Nobody agrees how big it is. The World Bank reported 46 million hectares announced by 2010, while a 2011 estimate put the area above 80 million hectares. A 2013 review warned the scale may be exaggerated. Critics point to weak {{ref:nature-econ-652}}, poor consultation and the turn to large industrial farms. They also cite local people displaced without adequate compensation. A World Bank study estimated that only 2 to 10 percent of land in Africa is formally tenured, which leaves many users exposed. The deals remain contested. Critics call them a form of neocolonialism, while host governments present them as development.

nature-res-151.title: Prior appropriation: first in time, first in right
nature-res-151.text: In Gold-Rush-era California, miners needed water and settled who got it with a simple rule: first come, first served. Prior appropriation is that rule for sharing water. The first person to take water for a beneficial use keeps the right to go on taking that amount for that use. The right is to withdraw water, not to own it, and it can be lost if left unused for a long time. In a shortage, senior users need not cut back. The rule spread across the arid western United States and has flaws. Users who leave part of their allotment unused risk losing it, so it discourages conservation, and most western water still goes to farming. Streams can become over-appropriated, holding more rights than water, so the newest users almost never get any. The doctrine has also historically excluded ecological uses, such as keeping water in a river for wildlife, though some places now accept them.

nature-res-154.title: Riparian rights: water shared by the riverbank
nature-res-154.text: In the eastern United States, owning land along a river brings a share of its water. That is riparian water rights, a system that divides water among the owners of land along a river, lake or other water body. It comes from English common law and is used in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the eastern United States. Every owner whose land touches the water may make reasonable use of it. In a shortage, shares usually follow the length of each owner's frontage. The rights cannot be sold apart from the land. Water cannot be moved out of the watershed without regard for downstream owners, who have a right to receive it undiminished in flow and quality. The arid western states mainly follow {{ref:nature-res-151}} instead.

nature-res-148.title: Peak water: the limits of a watery planet
nature-res-148.text: Earth holds an estimated 1.34 billion cubic kilometres of water, but 96.5% is salty and less than 1% is accessible to people. Peak water is the idea that the availability, quality and use of fresh water face growing limits. Peter Gleick and Meena Palaniappan defined it in 2010, separating peak renewable, peak non-renewable and peak ecological water. Their point is that sustainably managed water is becoming scarce. Fossil water behaves like oil, echoing {{ref:nature-res-222}}. Pumping it faster than nature refills it can in theory produce a Hubbert-type production peak. The Ogallala Aquifer, mined far faster than it refills, is a classic case. Saudi Arabia reached peak water in the early 1990s at more than 30 billion cubic metres a year and now produces about half that rate. Farming dominates demand, with 70% of freshwater use worldwide. Typically only 35% to 50% of irrigation water reaches the crops, and higher water prices have been shown to improve efficiency.

nature-res-126.title: The hidden costs of food
nature-res-126.text: The price on a supermarket shelf leaves out a lot. The hidden costs of food are the environmental, social and health costs of producing and eating it that food prices do not reflect, also called external costs. They are a form of {{ref:nature-found-031}}. Examples include food's share in climate change, farmworker poverty and diet-related illness, all paid for by society. Estimates of the total for global agrifood systems range from USD 12 trillion to USD 19 trillion a year. Hidden health costs alone come to USD 8.1 trillion. Some costs are easier to count than others. Greenhouse gas costs are fairly easy to measure, while effects on working conditions and communities are harder.

nature-res-136.title: Groundwater pollution: poison seeping down
nature-res-136.text: What spills on the ground can end up in a well. Groundwater pollution happens when pollutants released on the surface make their way into groundwater. Sources include on-site sanitation, landfill leachate, leaking sewers, petrol stations, fracking and overuse of farm fertilizer. Drawing water from deep aquifers sealed beneath a watertight layer gives more protection from contamination at the surface.

nature-res-134.title: Sinking ground: subsidence from groundwater pumping
nature-res-134.text: Water in the ground does more than wait to be pumped. Its pressure in the pores normally helps hold up the weight of the sediments above. Pump too much out, and the ground can sink or collapse. One estimate links 80% of serious US land subsidence problems to excessive groundwater extraction. The damage can last, because subsidence can permanently reduce an aquifer's storage capacity.

nature-res-135.title: Seawater intrusion: when the sea moves underground
nature-res-135.text: Along coasts, fresh groundwater floats on salt water like a lens. In sandy coastal aquifers, the fresh water sits about 12 metres thick for every 0.3 m of freshwater head, its height above sea level. Seawater intrusion is the movement of denser seawater into these aquifers. Overpumping lowers the aquifer's pressure and lets salt water in. Once salted, an aquifer can no longer reliably supply towns.

nature-res-110.title: Land-use regulation: the rules on what goes where
nature-res-110.text: New York City passed the first US zoning ordinance in 1916, and most states had zoning laws by the 1930s. Land-use regulation is the set of public rules, such as zoning, by which governments plan and control how land may be used. An urban growth boundary, a line beyond which a city may not spread, is another form. Public rules are only part of the picture, though. Most controls on land in the US actually come from private developers and individuals.

nature-res-144.title: Land-use planning: deciding what land is for
nature-res-144.text: Belts of protected countryside and urban growth boundaries ring many cities, holding back development from rural and farm land. They are tools of land-use planning, the process by which a central authority regulates how land may be used. It aims at better social and environmental outcomes and more efficient use of resources. Modern goals include conserving the environment, restraining urban sprawl, cutting transport costs, preventing land-use conflicts and limiting exposure to pollutants. It nearly always relies on {{ref:nature-res-110}}, typically zoning. Zoning controls what may happen on a piece of land and how buildings are placed and shaped. Planning also helps manage floods, alongside warning systems and {{ref:nature-clim-039}}. Its effects are contested. Planners assume rules change behavior, which is widely accepted. Whether those changes are beneficial is disputed and depends on place and rules. Critics say rules are often too strict, making land supply too slow to respond and pushing prices up sharply. In North America, they argue, planning systems have worsened housing crises.

nature-res-097.title: Plantation forestry: rows of one tree species
nature-res-097.text: A plantation can produce a lot of wood in a short time. Plantation forestry grows forests planted for high-volume wood production, usually as a single tree species. Industrial plantations are large and actively managed, made of blocks of one or two species all the same age. The uniformity has a cost. Plantations may support fewer pollinators than natural forests with varied structure.

nature-res-096.title: Proforestation: letting existing forests grow on
nature-res-096.text: Counting land clearing and short product lifetimes, plantations sequester 40 times less carbon than natural forests. Proforestation takes the opposite path. It protects existing natural forests so they keep growing, storing carbon and gaining complexity without harvesting. It complements planting new forests, replanting old ones and better forest management as forest-based climate solutions. Old-growth and complex forests also resist climate change effects and fire better than young ones, making them a lasting {{ref:nature-eco-169}}.

nature-res-121.title: Catchment factors: why some rivers flood
nature-res-121.text: Rain on roofs, pavements and roads reaches rivers with almost no absorption into the ground. That is one of several catchment factors, the features of a {{ref:nature-res-119}} that determine how likely it is to flood: topography, shape, size, soil type and land use. Topography and shape set how fast rain reaches the river. Size, soil and development set how much arrives. Sandy soils absorb rain, while clay soils are nearly impermeable and add to flood volumes.

nature-res-120.title: Endorheic basins: rivers that never reach the sea
nature-res-120.text: Around 18% of Earth's land drains nowhere near the ocean. An endorheic basin is an inland drainage basin whose water never reaches the sea. Where evaporation is the main way water leaves, it is usually saltier than the ocean, the Dead Sea being an extreme case. The largest such basins are in Central Asia, including the Caspian and Aral Seas.

nature-res-099.title: Water pricing: what a cubic meter should cost
nature-res-099.text: Piped water costs anywhere from US$0.01 to almost US$8 per cubic meter, depending on where a tap is. Water pricing is the various ways of setting a {{ref:nature-econ-356}} for water. Efficient pricing needs to know water's value in other uses, the private and external costs of supplying it, and the options for a tariff. Tariffs can be uniform or variable and flat or volumetric, charged by the amount used. That gives almost endless combinations. Utilities set their tariffs administratively. Irrigation water is usually charged a flat rate, because metering is uncommon on farms. Raising irrigation prices does not always cut use proportionally, especially when farmers lack money, efficient technology or other livelihoods. Some places let water rights be traded so a market sets the price, as in parts of Australia, Chile and the Southwestern United States.

nature-res-132.title: Forest genetic diversity: a forest's insurance
nature-res-132.text: No two trees in a forest are quite alike, and that matters. Forest genetic diversity is the DNA differences among forest trees, which keep forests healthy and adaptable. It gives resilience to pests and diseases and lets trees survive and evolve as conditions change. It is threatened by fire, habitat fragmentation, pests, poor {{ref:nature-res-156}} and unsuitable planting material.

nature-res-114.title: Confined and unconfined aquifers
nature-res-114.text: Whether an aquifer can swell with rain depends on what lies above it. Aquifers are classed by whether an impermeable layer, one water cannot pass, sits on top. An unconfined aquifer has no such barrier, so its water level can rise with recharge, and its top is the water table. A confined aquifer has an impermeable layer above it that stops its water level rising. The same rock unit may be confined in one place and unconfined in another.

nature-res-175.title: Forestry law: some of the oldest environmental rules
nature-res-175.text: Rules on forest use spanning generations are among the oldest long-term environmental policies, dating to customary law codified in the 14th century. Forestry law governs activities on designated forest land, mainly forest management and timber harvesting. It usually sets policies for public forests, such as {{ref:nature-res-145}}. It aims to protect resources and prevent clearing, logging, hunting and plant collecting, but often sets no clear limits on how much may be cut or how often. Since the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}, slowing climate change has become one of its goals.

nature-res-141.title: Factory farms: livestock packed at high density
nature-res-141.text: A single operation may hold hundreds of thousands of cows, hogs, turkeys or chickens, often indoors. Concentrated animal feeding operations raise livestock in confinement at high density, a practice often called factory farming. They are the extreme of {{ref:nature-res-140}}. They aim for maximum output at the lowest cost, and they have greatly increased animal food production.

nature-res-171.title: Water conflict: disputes over a shared resource
nature-res-171.text: The Middle East has only 1% of the world's fresh water for 5% of its population, and most of its rivers cross borders. Water conflict is violence or dispute over access to or control of water, or the use of water and water systems as weapons or targets. Wars over water alone are rare. Water is more often one cause of tension among several. Conflicts can be between countries sharing a river, sea or aquifer, or within one country, such as farmers against city users.

nature-res-170.title: Water risk: the flip side of water security
nature-res-170.text: Agriculture uses 69% of the world's freshwater, which puts whole industries on the line when water fails. Water risk is the possibility of water-related problems such as scarcity, stress, flooding, drought or decaying infrastructure. As risk rises, {{ref:nature-res-169}} falls. Like other kinds of {{ref:nature-econ-773}}, it combines {{ref:nature-clim-223}}. It threatens industries such as food and beverages, agriculture, oil and gas, and utilities.

nature-res-102.title: Water use by sector: farms, factories and homes
nature-res-102.text: Irrigation has been central to agriculture for over 5,000 years, and farms still take the lion's share of water. Water use by sector is how water is divided among uses such as irrigated farming, industry and households. Some need it only at times, others continuously. An estimated 22% of the world's water goes to industry, including power plant cooling, refineries and manufacturing. About 8% is used at home for drinking, cooking, bathing and cleaning. Industry may withdraw a lot of water, but it generally consumes much less than agriculture.

nature-res-103.title: Water resource management: who gets the water
nature-res-103.text: Many rivers and lakes are shared across national or internal borders, which makes fair management hard. Water resource management is the planning, development, distribution and management of the best use of water. Ideally it allocates water fairly among all competing demands. In practice decision-makers must put sustainability, equity and optimization first, in that order. Climate change adds uncertainty, so managers increasingly involve the people affected and build the ability to adapt. The sixth of the UN's sustainable-development goals aims to implement {{ref:nature-res-104}} at all levels by 2030.

nature-res-104.title: Integrated water resources management (IWRM)
nature-res-104.text: Water, land and the resources tied to them cannot be managed in separate boxes. Integrated water resources management, or IWRM, is a process that coordinates their development and management. It aims to maximize economic and social welfare fairly without harming vital ecosystems. It rests on three principles: social equity, economic efficiency and ecological sustainability. It emerged at international conferences in the late 1900s and early 2000s and was recommended in the 1992 Dublin Statement. Scholars see {{ref:nature-res-169}} as the goal and IWRM as the process to reach it. It is evolving to include the nexus approach, which recognizes that water, energy and food are closely linked. There is no single correct administrative model; practice depends on context.
